passage: I'm Kavitha, and I share the open-plan office with Usha, who manages our team. On Monday Usha sent Bhavna a one-line message: “Prepare the vendor summary by Wednesday.” Bhavna spent two days on a twelve-page comparison with charts. On Wednesday, Usha opened it, and her jaw tightened. “I wanted one page, for the board. This is a report.” Bhavna said quietly, “I didn't know it was for the board.” Usha sighed loudly and later muttered to me, “Some people just don't listen.” I couldn't say what Usha was feeling; maybe stress. But I remember that the message had no audience, no length and no purpose.

qa.q: By which day was the vendor summary due?
qa.a: The vendor summary was due by Wednesday.

qa.q: What might Usha have been feeling when her jaw tightened?
qa.a: Usha was probably frustrated and stressed, and blamed Bhavna for not listening, though Kavitha cannot see the inner state exactly.

qa.q: What could Usha do differently when handing over the next task?
qa.a: Say who the summary is for, how long it should be, what it is for and when it is due, and agree a quick check on Tuesday.

qa.q: How might Bhavna feel after two days of work and Usha's reaction?
qa.a: Bhavna probably feels confused and disheartened, since the effort was real and the one-line message did not say the audience.

grounding: A manager hands a task off with one line, expects the result in their head, and blames the person when it differs.

passage:
Monday: Dolma sent Bhavna a one-line message before a meeting: “Sort the client feedback.” Bhavna wasn't sure whether sort meant summarise, tag or reply, so she made a spreadsheet of sixty rows and sent it Tuesday night.

Wednesday: Dolma opened the file, sighed and said, “This is not what I meant. I needed the top three complaints.” Bhavna's face fell. “I didn't know that.” Dolma turned away and said, more sharply than she intended, “I don't know how else to say it.”

Friday: Dolma told a colleague, “I explained it, and she still got it wrong.”

qa.q: How many rows did Bhavna's spreadsheet have?
What was Dolma feeling when saying “I don't know how else to say it”?
qa.a: Dolma was irritated and frustrated, believing the instruction was clear; the sharp tone shows Dolma blames the person, though the message was the gap.

qa.q: What could Dolma do on Monday to prevent this result?
qa.a: Write what she wants, the top three complaints and who will read it, and say when it is due and when they will look at it together.

qa.q: How might Bhavna have felt when her face fell on Wednesday?
qa.a: Bhavna was probably confused and dismayed, since she had worked hard on a guess at what “sort” meant.

grounding: A person passes on a task with one line, expects it to match what was in their head and blames the other person when it does not.
